Comparing Sequences Between Groups: Early vs Late Human-AI Interactions

Mohammed Saqr

University of Eastern Finland

Sonsoles López-Pernas

University of Eastern Finland

Kamila Misiejuk

FernUniversität in Hagen, Germany
Source: vignettes/sequence-comparison.Rmd
sequence-comparison.Rmd

Two groups of sequences can differ at several levels: in how often each state occurs, in which state follows which, in summary indices of each sequence, and in the patterns of states they contain. Nestimate (Saqr, López-Pernas & Misiejuk 2026) compares sequences at each of these levels. This vignette applies them to one question: whether people direct an AI coding assistant differently in the first and the second half of a session. Temporal patterns within a learning episode have been used to study how students’ interactions and self-regulation develop over time (Saqr, Nouri & Fors 2019).

Question Function
States: are they used in different proportions? mosaic_test()
Transitions: do their probabilities differ? permutation()
Sequences: do their summary indices differ? sequence_metrics(group = )
Patterns: does a pattern occur more often? sequence_compare()
Patterns: does a pattern occur in more sequences? sequence_patterns()
Jointly: which patterns or indices distinguish the groups? pattern_outcome(), outcome_model()

Data

human_long holds the coded human turns of 429 human-AI pair-programming (“vibe coding”) sessions across 34 projects, one row per coded action (Saqr, Misiejuk & López-Pernas 2026; Misiejuk et al. 2026). The nine action codes are grouped into three clusters, Directive, Evaluative and Metacognitive, in the column cluster, which is the state used here. order_in_session gives the position of each action within its session.

mark_phases() orders the actions of each session by order_in_session and divides them into consecutive phases of nearly equal length. With n = 2, the first half of each session is labelled early and the second half late; with an odd number of actions, the middle one belongs to the second half.

library(Nestimate)
halves <- mark_phases(human_long, actor = "session_id",
                      time = "order_in_session", n = 2,
                      labels = c("early", "late"))

build_network() with group = "phase" estimates one transition network per half and keeps the half-session sequences, which every function below reads.

net <- build_network(halves, actor = "session_id", action = "cluster",
                     group = "phase", method = "relative")
net
#> Group Networks (2 groups, group_col: phase)
#> 
#>   Group  Nodes  Edges  Weights
#>   early  3      9      [0.105, 0.637]
#>   late   3      9      [0.131, 0.575]

There are 425 early and 429 late half-sessions; the four sessions with a single action have no early half.

Nested data

Every session contributes one early and one late half, and the actions of a session come from the same person, project and AI assistant. The observations are therefore nested in sessions, and a test that treats the actions or the half-sessions as independent overstates the evidence when sessions differ from each other. Each function below has an argument for the nesting: actor for the tests based on counts and permutations, which then correct for the clustering or shuffle the labels only within a session (Anderson & ter Braak 2003; Good 2005), and group for the regression models, which then include a random intercept for each session (Bates et al. 2015).

States

The first comparison concerns the share of each state, ignoring order. sequence_plot() with type = "distribution" shows the share of each state at each position of the half-sessions. With na = FALSE the shares are taken among the observed actions, and trim = 0.9 keeps the positions that hold 90% of the actions, since few half-sessions are longer.

sequence_plot(net, type = "distribution", na = FALSE, trim = 0.9)

Early halves start almost entirely with directives; late halves start with all three states, and metacognitive actions take a larger share of the late halves.

mosaic_test() cross-tabulates the half against the state and tests the association with every method for clustered counts. With actor = "session_id", the sessions are the clusters.

mosaic_test(net, actor = "session_id")
#>        method                    test statistic       df      df2      p_value
#> 1       chisq                 Pearson  69.78883 2.000000       NA 7.007264e-16
#> 2   rao_scott               Rao-Scott  28.72328 1.973638 844.7172 1.156606e-12
#> 3 donner_klar             Donner-Klar        NA       NA       NA           NA
#> 4         cmh Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel  74.24399 2.000000       NA 7.553064e-17
#> 5         gee                GEE Wald  58.16751 2.000000       NA 2.339297e-13
#> 6        glmm               GLMM Wald  69.33653 2.000000       NA 8.785453e-16
#>       n clusters design_effect icc
#> 1 10796       NA            NA  NA
#> 2 10796      429      1.214848  NA
#> 3 10796       NA            NA  NA
#> 4 10796      421            NA  NA
#> 5 10796      429            NA  NA
#> 6 10796      429            NA  NA
#>                                                                                                                                       note
#> 1                                                                                                                                     <NA>
#> 2                                                                                                                                     <NA>
#> 3                                                                     Donner-Klar needs one variable that is constant within every cluster
#> 4                                                                                                                                     <NA>
#> 5 Wald test with a cluster-robust covariance; liberal unless the actors are many relative to the degrees of freedom (see ?mosaic_analysis)
#> 6                                                                                                                                     <NA>

The Pearson chi-square test treats the 10,796 actions as independent. The Rao-Scott test corrects it for the clustering with a second-order adjustment (Rao & Scott 1984); the design effect, 1.21, is the factor by which the clustering inflates the variance. The Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel test stratifies by session and compares the halves within each of the 421 sessions that have both (Landis, Heyman & Koch 1978). The GEE test uses a cluster-robust covariance (Liang & Zeger 1986), and the GLMM test a mixed model with a random intercept per session. The Donner-Klar test needs one variable that is constant within each cluster (Donner & Klar 1994), and the half varies within every session, so it is not computed. The four tests that apply all reject independence (Rao-Scott F(1.97, 844.7) = 28.72, CMH = 74.24, GEE = 58.17, GLMM = 69.34; every p < 0.001).

mosaic_plot(net)

In the mosaic plot, the width of a column is the share of actions in each half and the height of a tile the share of each state within the half. The fill is the standardised residual: blue tiles hold more actions than independence predicts and red tiles fewer. Directives are over-represented early; evaluations and metacognitive actions late.

Transitions

The second comparison concerns the transition probabilities, the probability of each state following each state. permutation() compares the two networks edge by edge and as a whole by shuffling the early and late labels and recomputing the differences, which is the comparison used in transition network analysis (Saqr et al. 2025). With actor = "session_id", the labels are shuffled only within each session.

set.seed(2026)
transitions <- permutation(net, iter = 1000, actor = "session_id")
summary(transitions)
#>           group          from            to  weight_x  weight_y        diff
#> 1 early vs late     Directive     Directive 0.6368638 0.5752445  0.06161928
#> 2 early vs late     Directive    Evaluative 0.2032325 0.2449210 -0.04168853
#> 3 early vs late     Directive Metacognitive 0.1599037 0.1798345 -0.01993075
#> 4 early vs late    Evaluative     Directive 0.4547582 0.4901712 -0.03541302
#> 5 early vs late    Evaluative    Evaluative 0.4407176 0.3792010  0.06151661
#> 6 early vs late    Evaluative Metacognitive 0.1045242 0.1306278 -0.02610359
#> 7 early vs late Metacognitive     Directive 0.4494048 0.3964497  0.05295506
#> 8 early vs late Metacognitive    Evaluative 0.3690476 0.2875740  0.08147365
#> 9 early vs late Metacognitive Metacognitive 0.1815476 0.3159763 -0.13442871
#>   effect_size     p_value   sig
#> 1    4.767254 0.000999001  TRUE
#> 2   -3.424018 0.000999001  TRUE
#> 3   -2.005723 0.046953047  TRUE
#> 4   -1.813544 0.062937063 FALSE
#> 5    3.231657 0.002997003  TRUE
#> 6   -2.159258 0.027972028  TRUE
#> 7    2.060593 0.033966034  TRUE
#> 8    3.324027 0.002997003  TRUE
#> 9   -4.926942 0.000999001  TRUE

weight_x and weight_y are the transition probabilities of the early and the late half, diff their difference, and effect_size the difference divided by the standard deviation of the permuted differences. Eight of the nine transitions differ. The global statistic M, the sum of the absolute edge differences, is 0.515, and no permutation reached it (p = 0.001, the smallest value 1,000 permutations can give). The largest difference concerns a metacognitive action followed by another: its probability is 0.18 in the first half and 0.32 in the second.

Sequence indices

The third comparison summarises each half-session with indices of its composition and dynamics, such as the number of distinct states, the evenness of the states (longitudinal entropy), the share of consecutive actions that change state (transition rate) and the mean length of a spell in one state (Gabadinho et al. 2011). sequence_metrics() computes them for every sequence; for a grouped network it compares each index between the groups. For each index it reports the number of half-sessions, the mean and the standard deviation of each half; the difference between the means (late minus early); Hedges’ g, the standardised difference corrected for small samples, with its 95% interval (Hedges 1981); eta squared, the share of the index’s variance between the halves; and a permutation p-value of the one-way F statistic, adjusted with the Benjamini-Hochberg method. The network was built with actor = "session_id", so the labels are shuffled within each session.

set.seed(2026)
sequence_metrics(net)

Most indices differ between the halves. The largest differences concern the opening state: in the late halves it holds a smaller share of the half-session (initial_state_proportion, 0.67 against 0.51, g = -0.78 [-0.92, -0.64]) and is left sooner (initial_state_persistence, g = -0.70). Late halves change state more often (transition_rate, 0.41 against 0.55, g = 0.60 [0.46, 0.74]), spend less time in their dominant state (dominant_proportion, g = -0.53) and in each spell (mean_spell_duration, 2.22 against 1.86 actions, g = -0.41), and spread their actions more evenly (longitudinal_entropy, 0.61 against 0.74, g = 0.47; simpson_diversity, g = 0.50). self_loop_tendency is one minus the transition rate, so its test is the same. Three rows need no interpretation. The late half is never shorter than the early half, because mark_phases() puts the middle action of an odd-length session in the second half, so valid_n differs although the means are almost equal (12.4 against 12.8, g = 0.03). valid_proportion is 1 for every half-session and cannot be compared. The two indices of the emergent state are defined only for the half-sessions that have one (161 early, 240 late) and do not differ.

Patterns

A pattern is a sequence of consecutive states, such as Directive->Directive->Evaluative, a k-gram of length 3. The halves can differ in how often a pattern occurs, which weighs each half-session by how often it repeats the pattern, and in how many half-sessions contain it, which counts each half-session once.

How often a pattern occurs

For each pattern length in sub (3 to 5 by default), sequence_compare() counts every pattern in each half and keeps the patterns that occur at least min_freq times in both. The standardised residual compares a half’s count with the count expected if pattern and half were independent, in approximately standard-normal units (Haberman 1973). The permutation test shuffles the labels within sessions (actor), and the p-values are adjusted with the false discovery rate (Benjamini & Hochberg 1995).

set.seed(20260413)
counts <- sequence_compare(net, min_freq = 25L, test = "permutation",
                           iter = 1000L, actor = "session_id")
counts
#> Sequence Comparison  [100 patterns | 2 groups: early, late]
#>   Lengths: 3, 4, 5  |  min_freq: 25  |  permutation: 1000 iter (fdr), actor: session_id (429 actors, mixed)

The printout shows one row per pattern and half: count is how often the pattern occurs in the half, prop its share of the half’s patterns of that length, resid the standardised residual, and effect the number of standard deviations by which the observed statistic exceeds the mean of the permuted ones; effect and p belong to the pattern and repeat on its two rows. summary(counts, format = "long") returns that table for every pattern, and summary(counts) one row per pattern. Of the 100 patterns tested, 18 differ at a false discovery rate of 0.05: 11 are more frequent early and 7 late. Directives followed by a metacognitive action are more frequent early (Directive->Directive->Directive->Metacognitive, 278 against 149), and patterns that start with an evaluation and continue with directives are more frequent late (Evaluative->Directive->Directive, 265 against 379).

plot(counts, style = "pyramid", show_residuals = TRUE)

The pyramid shows the patterns with the largest differences, the first half on the left and the second on the right, each pattern’s count beside its bar, its residual inside the bar when the bar is wide enough, and its p-value in the middle. The heatmap shows the same residuals as a grid of patterns by halves, the layout used for more than two groups.

plot(counts, style = "heatmap")

By default the patterns are ranked by the test statistic; sort = "frequency" ranks them by their total count instead, which shows the most common patterns whatever their difference.

plot(counts, style = "pyramid", sort = "frequency", show_residuals = TRUE)

How many sequences contain a pattern

Support is the share of sequences that contain a pattern at least once (Agrawal & Srikant 1995). sequence_patterns() reports the support of each pattern and, for a group of networks, compares it between the groups with Fisher’s exact test and an odds ratio with its 95% interval; the odds ratios are those of the late half, and p_adj is adjusted with the Benjamini-Hochberg method. Fisher’s test treats the half-sessions as independent samples, so these p-values do not take the sessions into account. Four kinds of pattern are compared.

Contiguous patterns 

ngrams <- sequence_patterns(net, type = "ngram", len = 3:4, min_freq = 25)
ngrams

Of the 95 patterns, 20 differ in support at an adjusted level of 0.05: 8 occur in a larger share of early halves and 12 in a larger share of late halves. Directive->Directive->Directive occurs in 88% of the early halves and 59% of the late halves (odds ratio 0.20 [0.13, 0.28]), and Evaluative->Directive->Directive in 37% and 54% (2.01 [1.51, 2.67]).

Two states with others between them

A gapped pattern fixes two states and allows any states between them: Evaluative->*->Directive is an evaluation followed by a directive two positions later, Evaluative->**->Directive three positions later.

gaps <- sequence_patterns(net, type = "gapped", gap = 1:2, min_freq = 25)
gaps

Of the 18 gapped patterns, 10 differ. An evaluation is followed by a directive two or three positions later in more late halves (47% against 65%, odds ratio 2.05 [1.54, 2.72]; 39% against 60%, 2.33 [1.76, 3.10]), and a directive by a directive two positions later in more early halves (92% against 77%, 0.27 [0.17, 0.42]).

Repetitions of one state

A repeated pattern is a repetition of one state. Comparing repetitions of increasing length shows whether a group persists in a state for longer.

repeats <- sequence_patterns(net, type = "repeated", len = 2:5,
                             min_freq = 10)
repeats

Of the 12 repetitions, 7 differ. Repetitions of two to four directives occur in a larger share of early halves. Repetitions of metacognitive actions occur in a larger share of late halves, and the odds ratio grows with the length of the repetition: 1.94 for two, 2.56 for three, 3.77 for four and 10.10 for five. The repetition of five occurs in 1 early and 10 late half-sessions, so its interval is wide ([1.43, 439.30]). Repetitions of evaluations do not differ.

The instances of one template

pattern = searches for the instances of one template, in which * matches any one state, and start, end and contain restrict the search to patterns that begin, end or include given states.

sequence_patterns(net, pattern = "Evaluative->*->Directive")
#> Sequence patterns by phase  [3 patterns | 2 groups: early, late]
#>   presence test: Fisher's exact, odds ratio against early (BH)
#> 
#>  pattern                              n_sequences support group group_support

#>  Evaluative->Evaluative->Directive    268         0.31    late  0.35

All three instances of Evaluative->*->Directive occur in a larger share of late halves: an evaluation followed by a directive and another directive (37% against 54%), by another evaluation and a directive (27% against 35%), and by a metacognitive action and a directive (10% against 14%).

Joint models

The comparisons above test each pattern on its own, and patterns overlap: every half that contains Directive->Directive->Directive also contains Directive->Directive. pattern_outcome() fits one logistic regression in which the half is the outcome and the presence of each selected pattern is a predictor, so each pattern’s odds ratio is adjusted for the others, with a random intercept per session (group = "session_id"). It follows analyze_outcome() in codyna (Tikka, López-Pernas & Saqr 2026): the n patterns with the largest chi-square statistic are selected and entered together.

joint <- pattern_outcome(net, outcome = "phase", len = 2:3, n = 8,
                         group = "session_id")
joint

estimate is the log odds ratio of the late half, adjusted for the other patterns, and odds_ratio with or_lower and or_upper its exponent and 95% Wald interval. Four of the eight patterns remain associated with the half. A half that contains Directive->Directive->Directive (odds ratio 0.17 [0.11, 0.25]) or Directive->Directive->Metacognitive (0.53 [0.38, 0.74]) is less likely to be a late half; a half with Evaluative->Directive->Directive (2.42 [1.53, 3.81]) or Metacognitive->Metacognitive (2.13 [1.37, 3.30]) is more likely to be one. The other four have intervals that include 1 once the patterns above are in the model. The session variance is again estimated as zero. The patterns were selected by their association with the outcome before the model was fitted, so the p-values overstate the evidence.

The same kind of model relates the half to several sequence indices at once. outcome_model() fits a logistic regression of the half on the indices returned by sequence_metrics() with meta = TRUE, which keeps the half and the session of each sequence, with a random intercept per session (group = "session_id"; Bates et al. 2015). Three indices are entered: unique_states, longitudinal_entropy and transition_rate.

indices <- sequence_metrics(net, meta = TRUE)
index_model <- outcome_model(indices, outcome = "phase",
                             predictors = c("unique_states",
                                            "longitudinal_entropy",
                                            "transition_rate"),
                             group = "session_id")
index_model
#> Outcome Model
#> =============
#> Outcome  : phase | binomial 
#> Units    : 841 in 423 groups 
#> Terms    : 3  
#> p-values : BH corrected
#> 
#>                   term estimate std_error statistic ci_lower ci_upper
#> 1        unique_states   -1.013     0.296    -3.422   -1.593   -0.433
#> 2 longitudinal_entropy    3.050     0.814     3.746    1.454    4.646
#> 3      transition_rate    1.848     0.465     3.974    0.936    2.759
#>        p_value        p_adj odds_ratio or_lower or_upper
#> 1 6.212835e-04 0.0006212835      0.363    0.203    0.649
#> 2 1.797093e-04 0.0002695639     21.114    4.281  104.142
#> 3 7.068437e-05 0.0002120531      6.346    2.551   15.787

The model uses 841 half-sessions from 423 sessions; the 13 half-sessions with a single action have no transition rate. The odds ratios are those of a late half per unit of each index, each adjusted for the other two. A half with a higher entropy (odds ratio 21.1 per unit, 95% interval [4.3, 104.1]) or a higher transition rate (6.35 [2.55, 15.79]) is more likely to be a late half: late halves spread their actions more evenly over the states and switch between them more often. For the same entropy and transition rate, a half with more distinct states is less likely to be a late half (0.36 [0.20, 0.65]). The variance of the session intercepts is estimated as zero (a singular fit), so the halves of one session are no more alike than halves of different sessions once the indices are known.

plot(index_model)

Summary

The levels agree. Early in a session, people give more directives, in long repetitions that stay in the opening state; later, they change state more often, spread their actions more evenly over the states, follow an evaluation with a directive more often and repeat metacognitive actions more often. The state tests, the permutation tests of the transitions, indices and pattern counts, and the mixed models take the sessions into account; the Fisher tests of pattern support do not.
